title: Understanding Beat-to-Beat Variations in P-Wave Morphology Among Atrial Fibrillation Patients During Sinus Rhythm: A Scoping Survey of Atrial Simulation Studies

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: P-wave physiology and atrial depolarization
subsections.content:
The surface P wave represents the spatiotemporal summation of atrial depolarization during sinus rhythm. Activation normally begins in the sinoatrial node region, spreads across the right atrium, and reaches the left atrium predominantly through preferential interatrial connections, especially Bachmann’s bundle; the recorded waveform therefore reflects the direction, synchrony, and velocity of propagation rather than a simple measure of atrial size alone ref [1], ref [2]. Experimental and clinical mapping studies established that alterations in atrial conduction pathways can change P-wave duration, axis, and contour even when rhythm remains sinus ref [1], ref [3].

Classically, the early portion of the P wave is weighted toward right atrial activation, whereas the terminal portion contains greater left atrial contribution; delayed or fragmented left atrial activation can produce widening, notching, or biphasic morphology, particularly in inferior leads and V1 ref [4], ref [5]. Quantitative descriptors such as P-wave duration, dispersion, terminal force in V1, and signal-averaged indices have therefore been used as noninvasive surrogates of conduction heterogeneity and atrial abnormality ref [5], ref [6].

Importantly, normal P-wave morphology is not perfectly fixed from beat to beat. Small variations arise from respiration, autonomic tone, subtle shifts in sinoatrial exit, and cycle-length dependent conduction properties, whereas larger or more complex variability may indicate anisotropic conduction, interatrial block, or localized conduction slowing within remodeled atrial tissue ref [2], ref [7], ref [8]. This physiological framework is essential for interpreting P-wave variability as a potential marker of latent atrial substrate relevant to atrial fibrillation.

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Atrial fibrillation substrate during sinus rhythm
subsections.content:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is sustained by a structural and functional atrial substrate that is often already present during sinus rhythm. Experimental and clinical work has shown that AF-related remodeling includes myocyte dedifferentiation, fibrosis, gap-junction alterations, and anisotropic conduction, creating a chamber in which apparently normal sinus activation masks substantial spatial heterogeneity ref [9], ref [10]. In this sense, the sinus-rhythm P wave can be viewed as the surface ECG projection of a remodeled atrium rather than a purely normal depolarization pattern.

Electroanatomic studies support this concept by demonstrating low-voltage areas, conduction delay, fractionation, and regional conduction slowing in patients with paroxysmal and persistent AF even when they are in sinus rhythm ref [11], ref [12]. Delayed enhancement MRI further links sinus-rhythm abnormalities to underlying atrial fibrosis, with greater fibrosis burden associated with more advanced disease and poorer outcomes after ablation ref [13], ref [14]. Histopathological observations are concordant, indicating that collagen deposition and discontinuous fiber coupling provide a substrate for nonuniform impulse propagation and local activation instability ref [15].

Accordingly, sinus rhythm in AF patients should not be interpreted as electrically homogeneous. Instead, beat-to-beat P-wave variability may reflect dynamic recruitment of alternate conduction pathways across a fixed but spatially complex substrate, modulated by cycle length, autonomic tone, and concealed conduction. This framework is consistent with the broader concept of electropathology in which subtle surface-ECG fluctuations mirror microstructural and conduction abnormalities that predispose to AF initiation and maintenance ref [16], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical significance of beat-to-beat morphological variation
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat variation in P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm is clinically meaningful because it may reveal intermittent changes in atrial conduction that are not captured by conventional summary measures such as mean P-wave duration. Experimental and clinical work has linked abnormal atrial conduction, anisotropy, and regional conduction delay to vulnerability for atrial fibrillation, supporting the concept that dynamic surface-ECG variability can act as a noninvasive marker of an unstable atrial substrate ref [18], ref [19]. In this framework, fluctuating P-wave shape reflects variable engagement of preferential conduction pathways, localized slowing, or shifting sites of earliest activation within remodeled atrial tissue.

Its significance is reinforced by studies showing that ECG manifestations of atrial conduction abnormality predict incident or recurrent AF. Interatrial block and advanced P-wave abnormalities are associated with supraventricular arrhythmias and adverse outcomes ref [4], ref [20]. Likewise, abnormal P-wave indices, including prolonged duration and abnormal terminal force in V1, have been related to future AF in population cohorts ref [21], ref [22]. Signal-averaged and high-resolution analyses further suggest that subtle atrial late potentials and low-amplitude components identify delayed or fragmented activation not visible on routine inspection ref [23], ref [24].

Accordingly, beat-to-beat morphological variation may have value beyond static P-wave descriptors: it could indicate temporally unstable conduction and latent remodeling even when average P-wave metrics remain borderline. This makes such variability potentially useful for identifying patients with concealed atrial cardiomyopathy, refining post-ablation or post-stroke risk assessment, and complementing structural imaging and rhythm monitoring in AF phenotyping ref [20], ref [22], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Distinguishing normal variability from pathological heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Some beat-to-beat P-wave variation is physiological. Respiration, autonomic fluctuation, minor shifts in sinus node exit site, and noise-sensitive delineation can alter amplitude, axis, and duration without implying structural disease. This normal lability is typically small, temporally smooth, and accompanied by preserved global indices of atrial conduction. In contrast, pathological heterogeneity is suggested when variability coexists with prolonged P-wave duration, increased dispersion, abnormal terminal forces, or interatrial block patterns, all of which have been linked to delayed and nonuniform atrial activation in patients with atrial remodeling or atrial fibrillation susceptibility ref [26], ref [27], ref [28].

A practical distinction therefore depends on whether morphology variation reflects benign modulation of a stable activation pathway or switching among impaired conduction routes. Signal-averaged and high-resolution studies show that diseased atria more often exhibit low-amplitude, fragmented, or prolonged atrial potentials, consistent with conduction discontinuity and anisotropy rather than simple physiologic fluctuation ref [29], ref [30]. Surface-ECG markers such as advanced interatrial block and abnormal P-terminal force in V1 further support the interpretation that variable P-wave shape may arise from latent substrate, particularly fibrosis and atrial enlargement ref [31], ref [32].

Accordingly, pathological variability should be interpreted probabilistically and in context: repeated occurrence across recordings, persistence after careful preprocessing, and association with AF-related outcomes favor substrate-mediated heterogeneity over normal variability. This view is consistent with work linking excessive P-wave dispersion and other atrial electrical markers to incident or recurrent AF, although these indices remain influenced by recording methodology and observer variability ref [33], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for diagnosis and risk stratification
subsections.content:
From a diagnostic perspective, beat-to-beat P-wave variability during sinus rhythm is attractive because it may expose atrial conduction disorder before sustained arrhythmia is documented. Conventional ECG markers such as prolonged P-wave duration and abnormal terminal force already track atrial remodeling and future atrial fibrillation risk in population studies, but they summarize a single averaged phenotype rather than dynamic instability ref [35], ref [36], ref [37]. Morphological variation across consecutive beats could therefore add information on intermittent conduction slowing, shifting breakthrough sites, or anisotropic propagation that remain occult on standard measurements.

This has direct implications for risk stratification. Excessive P-wave heterogeneity is conceptually aligned with the electropathological substrate associated with incident AF, stroke, and adverse outcomes, extending observations that advanced interatrial block and amplified P-wave duration identify patients with heightened arrhythmic vulnerability ref [4], ref [38], ref [39]. In cohorts undergoing rhythm monitoring or ablation, indices of atrial electrical instability may help enrich pretest probability for paroxysmal AF, refine selection for prolonged ambulatory monitoring, and complement echocardiographic or clinical scores rather than replace them.

The strongest near-term role is likely multimarker integration. Because P-wave morphology is inexpensive and repeatedly measurable, variability features could be combined with age, atrial size, natriuretic peptides, and established ECG phenotypes to improve prediction of AF recurrence after cardioversion or catheter ablation, where recurrence remains linked to underlying atrial remodeling ref [40], ref [41], ref [42]. For clinically useful deployment, however, diagnostic thresholds must be standardized against normal respiratory and autonomic variation, and incremental value should be demonstrated beyond conventional ECG and imaging markers.

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Changes
subsections.subsection_title: Anatomical determinants of atrial activation patterns
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm is strongly constrained by atrial anatomy because the surface P wave is the summed projection of right- and left-atrial activation vectors. Classic mapping studies showed that the dominant route of interatrial propagation is not fixed to a single pathway: preferential conduction may occur through Bachmann’s bundle, the fossa ovalis region, or muscular connections near the coronary sinus, each producing different left-atrial breakthrough patterns and therefore different P-wave axes and terminal forces ref [43], ref [44]. The contribution of these pathways is further shaped by the anisotropic architecture of atrial bundles and by chamber geometry, which determine local source-sink relations and activation timing ref [45], ref [46].

Interindividual variation in atrial size and bundle orientation provides an anatomic substrate for subtle lability even in nominal sinus rhythm. Detailed anatomic analyses of Bachmann’s bundle and adjacent septal structures have emphasized substantial variability in fiber arrangement and continuity, while electrocardiographic studies link advanced interatrial block to altered P-wave duration and morphology, consistent with rerouting of activation when preferential superior connections are delayed or interrupted ref [3], ref [47]. Imaging and electroanatomic work also show that atrial dilation and altered chamber curvature modify activation trajectories and prolong conduction paths, increasing the sensitivity of the P wave to small beat-to-beat changes in origin or conduction balance ref [48], ref [49].

In patients with atrial fibrillation, these anatomic determinants are especially important because pre-existing enlargement, altered septopulmonary relationships, and heterogeneous muscular sleeves around the venous inflows can amplify minor shifts in sinus node exit or intra-atrial conduction into measurable morphology changes. Thus, anatomy does not merely provide a static backdrop; it sets the preferential pathways, vector summation, and reserve of interatrial coupling that govern how small dynamic perturbations are expressed on the body surface ref [44], ref [46], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Changes
subsections.subsection_title: Fibrosis and microstructural remodeling
subsections.content:
Fibrosis and microstructural remodeling are central determinants of beat-to-beat variation in atrial activation because they alter local source–sink relations and fragment preferential conduction pathways. Histological and imaging studies in atrial fibrillation have shown that collagen deposition is not spatially uniform but concentrated in patchy interstitial and replacement patterns, particularly in the posterior left atrium and around the pulmonary veins, creating anisotropic conduction and local conduction delay ref [51], ref [52]. By changing the balance between longitudinal and transverse coupling, fibrosis can shift breakthrough sites and interatrial propagation sequences enough to produce subtle P-wave morphology differences even during apparent sinus rhythm ref [53].

At the microscale, remodeling is not limited to collagen accumulation. Myocyte loss, fibroblast proliferation, altered gap-junction distribution, and discontinuous fiber architecture promote zig-zag conduction and enhance susceptibility to functional block ref [54], ref [55]. Experimental and computational work has further shown that the arrhythmogenic impact of fibrosis depends on its texture and percolation properties rather than simply total burden, with diffuse versus patchy fibrosis producing different effects on wavefront continuity and electrogram complexity ref [56], ref [57]. These same properties are expected to destabilize sinus-wavefront propagation from beat to beat when cycle length, autonomic input, or premature activity slightly changes local excitability.

Clinically, delayed-enhancement MRI studies support a link between structural remodeling burden and altered atrial conduction phenotype, although the relationship is imperfect because macroscopic fibrosis is filtered through underlying fiber orientation and chamber geometry ref [58], ref [59]. Thus, microstructural remodeling provides a substrate in which small physiological perturbations can be amplified into observable beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variability.

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Changes
subsections.subsection_title: Regional conduction abnormalities
subsections.content:
Regional conduction abnormalities are a major source of beat-to-beat P-wave variability because they alter the sequence and timing of right- and left-atrial depolarization even during apparent sinus rhythm. High-density epicardial mapping has shown that patients with atrial fibrillation frequently exhibit localized conduction delay, conduction block, and complex activation at Bachmann’s bundle, the crista terminalis, and the posterior left atrium, regions that normally coordinate interatrial propagation ref [60], ref [61]. When conduction through these preferential pathways becomes discontinuous, the relative contribution of alternative routes changes from beat to beat, producing subtle shifts in P-wave axis, duration, and terminal forces.

These abnormalities are not simply fixed scars but often reflect anisotropic and rate-sensitive conduction in structurally remodeled tissue. Experimental and clinical studies have demonstrated that nonuniform anisotropy and discontinuous cell-to-cell coupling can promote zig-zag conduction and localized delay, particularly where fiber architecture changes abruptly or fibrosis is patchy ref [62], ref [63]. In AF substrates, such abnormalities are accentuated by atrial dilation and remodeling, and signal-averaged or body-surface markers of prolonged or fractionated atrial activation are consistent with this substrate ref [30], ref [10]. As a result, small cycle-length variations or shifts in sinus exit can recruit different conduction channels across successive beats.

Interatrial conduction disturbance is especially relevant to P-wave morphology. Advanced interatrial block, classically linked to Bachmann bundle impairment, produces characteristic changes in P-wave duration and polarity and is strongly associated with atrial arrhythmia vulnerability ref [64]. More broadly, endo-epicardial dissociation and asynchronous activation in remodeled atria can further diversify the surface projection of atrial depolarization ref [65]. Thus, regional conduction abnormalities provide a mechanistic bridge between microstructural remodeling and dynamic, beat-to-beat P-wave morphological variation in patients with AF history during sinus rhythm.

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Changes
subsections.subsection_title: Sinus node and atrial ectopic influence
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat P-wave variation during nominal sinus rhythm can arise from instability of the dominant atrial pacemaker. The human sinus node is a distributed complex rather than a point source, and shifts in the site of earliest activation along the crista terminalis or within the paranodal region can alter the initial activation vector and P-wave polarity or duration ref [66], ref [67]. High-resolution mapping studies further show that sinoatrial conduction into the atrial myocardium occurs through preferential exit pathways; intermittent use of different exits can therefore change right atrial breakthrough patterns without requiring a change in gross rhythm classification ref [68].

In atrial fibrillation patients, remodeling of the sinus node region and surrounding atrial tissue may accentuate this lability. Structural and functional abnormalities of the node and its atrial connections are well documented in sick sinus syndrome and AF-associated atrial cardiomyopathy, providing a substrate for pacemaker shift, sinoatrial exit block, and variable intra-atrial conduction ref [69], ref [70]. These mechanisms can generate subtle cycle-to-cycle differences in activation sequence that appear on the surface ECG as changing P-wave morphology even when RR intervals remain relatively stable.

Atrial ectopic activity is an additional source of morphological variability. Premature atrial depolarizations, especially from pulmonary veins, the crista terminalis, coronary sinus, or low atrial sites, can transiently capture the atria or reset the sinus node, producing fusion or altered atrial activation on the subsequent beat ref [71], ref [72]. The relevance of ectopic triggers is underscored by seminal observations that AF is often initiated by rapid firing from the pulmonary veins ref [73], while focal ectopic atrial tachycardias from multiple right- and left-atrial locations generate characteristic but site-dependent P-wave patterns ref [74]. Accordingly, intermittent competition between sinus impulse formation and ectopic atrial activity is a plausible contributor to beat-to-beat P-wave morphology changes in AF patients during apparent sinus rhythm.

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Changes
subsections.subsection_title: Autonomic and rate-dependent modulation
subsections.content:
Autonomic fluctuations can modify P-wave morphology on a beat-to-beat basis by changing the site of impulse initiation, intra-atrial conduction velocity, and regional refractoriness. Experimental and clinical studies show that vagal activation abbreviates atrial action potential duration and effective refractory period with marked spatial heterogeneity, thereby favoring local conduction delay and shifting activation pathways, whereas sympathetic stimulation accelerates automaticity and can facilitate nonuniform anisotropic propagation ref [75], ref [76], ref [77]. In patients predisposed to atrial fibrillation, these short-term autonomic effects may be sufficient to alter the relative contribution of superior-inferior and right-left atrial breakthrough patterns during otherwise sinus rhythm.

Rate dependence further amplifies morphology variability. As cycle length shortens, sodium-channel recovery and source-sink balance become less favorable in diseased atrial tissue, promoting decremental conduction, anisotropy, and intermittent block; restitution-related changes in atrial refractoriness can therefore produce different activation sequences from one beat to the next even without a change in gross anatomy ref [78], ref [79]. This is particularly relevant in remodeled atria, where conduction slowing is accentuated at faster rates and may unmask latent lines of functional block or preferential conduction bundles ref [80], ref [81].

Autonomic and rate-dependent mechanisms are tightly coupled. Heart-rate acceleration during sympathetic surges, or vagally mediated bradycardia with increased dispersion of refractoriness, can both destabilize sinoatrial exit and favor competing atrial pacemaker activity or ectopic capture, each capable of changing P-wave polarity, duration, and terminal forces ref [76], ref [77], ref [82]. Accordingly, beat-to-beat P-wave variability in atrial fibrillation patients during sinus rhythm should be interpreted not only as a marker of fixed substrate, but also as a dynamic readout of transient neurohumoral state superimposed on structural remodeling ref [81], ref [83].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Changes
subsections.subsection_title: Interplay between electrical and structural remodeling
subsections.content:
Electrical and structural remodeling are tightly coupled in atrial fibrillation and together provide a substrate for beat-to-beat P-wave variability during sinus rhythm. Structural changes such as interstitial fibrosis, myocyte hypertrophy, and altered cell-to-cell coupling slow and spatially fragment atrial conduction, while electrical remodeling shortens refractoriness and modifies excitability, increasing the sensitivity of activation sequences to small shifts in sinus exit or preferential conduction pathways ref [10], ref [55]. Experimental and clinical work indicates that this coupling is not merely additive: fibrosis amplifies local source–sink mismatch and favors discontinuous propagation, so modest dynamic changes in cycle length or autonomic state can produce visible changes in P-wave morphology ref [84], ref [73].

At the tissue level, connexin remodeling and anisotropic discontinuity are important interfaces between electrical and structural disease. Reduced or heterogeneous connexin expression, particularly involving Cx40 and Cx43, has been linked to slowed transverse conduction and increased conduction inhomogeneity in human atria ref [85], ref [86]. These abnormalities often coexist with fibroblast accumulation and extracellular matrix expansion, which further alter electrotonic loading and may destabilize activation emerging from the sinoatrial region or ectopic atrial foci ref [55], ref [85].

Clinically, imaging- and mapping-based studies support the view that the extent and spatial distribution of atrial fibrosis shape electrical complexity and conduction behavior. Delayed-enhancement MRI correlates with electroanatomic abnormalities and AF stage, while high-density mapping demonstrates endo-epicardial dissociation and conduction disorder in remodeled atria ref [87], ref [88]. Thus, beat-to-beat P-wave morphology changes in AF patients during sinus rhythm can be interpreted as surface manifestations of a dynamic interaction between fixed structural barriers and labile electrophysiological properties, rather than as consequences of either process alone ref [10], ref [88], ref [89].

subsections.section_title: Atrial Simulation Frameworks for Studying P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Cellular and tissue electrophysiology models
subsections.content:
Cellular atrial electrophysiology models provide the mechanistic basis for simulating beat-to-beat P-wave variability because they determine action-potential duration, excitability, and rate adaptation at the source level. Human atrial ionic models have evolved from early formulations emphasizing repolarizing current balance to more detailed descriptions of calcium handling and region-dependent kinetics, notably the Courtemanche model, the Nygren model, and later refinements by Maleckar and Koivumäki that improved agreement with human atrial recordings under different pacing conditions and subcellular calcium dynamics [1,2,3,4]. These models are particularly valuable when probing how subtle fluctuations in automaticity, refractoriness, or conduction reserve may alter activation sequence without requiring gross anatomical change.

At tissue scale, monodomain or bidomain formulations couple these ionic models to anisotropic propagation, allowing investigation of how fiber orientation, intercellular coupling, and spatial heterogeneity shape atrial depolarization and, consequently, P-wave morphology. A key advance was the incorporation of regional electrophysiological heterogeneity and realistic conduction architecture into atrial tissue frameworks, including the Crista Terminalis, pectinate muscles, and Bachmann’s bundle, which strongly influence sinus activation patterns and interatrial delay [5,6]. Such models can reproduce normal and perturbed atrial breakthrough sequences and are therefore well suited to isolating whether morphology variability arises from altered sinus node exit, localized conduction slowing, or transient block.

For studies of variability linked to disease, cellular remodeling modules are often superimposed on these tissue models. Chronic atrial fibrillation remodeling shortens refractoriness and modifies conduction through changes in ionic currents and structural coupling, effects captured in computational studies that connect ionic remodeling to altered wavefront propagation and ECG manifestations [7,8]. More recent populations-of-models approaches further acknowledge inter-subject and beat-to-beat uncertainty by varying ionic conductances within experimentally plausible ranges, enabling sensitivity analyses of which cellular determinants most strongly modulate activation timing and P-wave features [9].

subsections.section_title: Atrial Simulation Frameworks for Studying P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Anatomically detailed atrial models
subsections.content:
Anatomically detailed atrial models provide the structural substrate needed to study how local conduction heterogeneity is transformed into beat-to-beat differences in simulated P-wave morphology. A major advance was the construction of realistic three-dimensional atrial geometries from imaging and anatomical dissection, including explicit representation of the crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, Bachmann’s bundle, and interatrial connections, which strongly shape activation sequence and surface potentials ref [90], ref [91]. These models established that even under nominal sinus rhythm, modest changes in breakthrough site or preferential bundle conduction can alter P-wave duration, polarity, and notching.

Subsequent frameworks incorporated rule-based or histology-informed fiber architecture and regional electrophysiological heterogeneity, enabling more faithful reproduction of anisotropic propagation and source–sink effects ref [92], ref [93]. Large human atrial models developed for arrhythmia research further emphasized the importance of wall thickness variation, trabeculation, and fibrosis distribution for conduction pathways and activation synchrony ref [94], ref [95]. Although many of these studies focused on atrial tachyarrhythmias, the same anatomical determinants are directly relevant for sinus activation and therefore for the subtle variability of the P wave.

For P-wave investigations, anatomically detailed models are especially valuable because they allow controlled perturbation of single structural features that are difficult to isolate clinically, such as the number and location of sinoatrial exits, interatrial bundle integrity, or regional dilation ref [96], ref [97]. Population-based statistical shape modeling has extended this paradigm by quantifying how inter-subject anatomical variability alone can modulate simulated atrial activation and ECG phenotypes ref [98].

subsections.section_title: Atrial Simulation Frameworks for Studying P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Patient-specific versus generic simulations
subsections.content:
A central modeling choice in studies of P-wave morphology variability is whether to use generic atrial geometries with population-averaged electrophysiology or patient-specific reconstructions derived from imaging and clinical mapping. Generic models are attractive because they permit controlled perturbation studies, standardized comparison across laboratories, and efficient exploration of how anatomy, fiber arrangement, and sinoatrial exit sites shape atrial activation and body-surface signals. This strategy underpins many mechanistic whole-atria simulations, including anatomically realistic human models developed for sinus rhythm and arrhythmia research ref [99], ref [100]. However, generic frameworks necessarily smooth inter-individual differences in atrial size, regional wall thickness, bundle architecture, and fibrosis burden that can materially alter P-wave duration, axis, and terminal force.

Patient-specific simulations seek to recover these individualized determinants by integrating segmented atrial anatomy, personalized fiber fields or rule-based surrogates, and, in some cases, clinical activation data or late-gadolinium enhancement MRI. Such pipelines have been especially influential in atrial fibrillation modeling, where image-based fibrosis and anatomy substantially affect conduction pathways and electrocardiographic manifestations ref [101], ref [102]. Multi-center efforts such as the CEMRG challenge further showed that patient-specific atrial anatomy can improve reproducibility of electrophysiological predictions while also exposing uncertainties related to mesh generation, fibrosis thresholds, and parameter tuning ref [103]. For P-wave studies, this means personalization can increase physiological fidelity, but only if the added parameters are identifiable from available data.

In practice, the two approaches are complementary rather than competing. Generic populations are well suited for sensitivity analysis, uncertainty quantification, and generation of synthetic ECG libraries spanning plausible atrial phenotypes ref [104], ref [105]. Patient-specific models are more appropriate when the objective is to explain observed morphology in an individual, estimate latent substrate, or assess intervention consequences under remodeled sinus rhythm ref [102], ref [106]. A pragmatic emerging view is to embed patient-specific anatomy within calibrated population-based electrophysiological priors, thereby balancing interpretability, data demands, and computational cost ref [103], ref [107].

subsections.section_title: Atrial Simulation Frameworks for Studying P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Forward modeling of surface ECG and P-wave synthesis
subsections.content:
Forward modeling provides the essential link between simulated atrial activation and observable P-wave morphology. In most atrial frameworks, transmembrane or equivalent source quantities are projected to the torso through the bidomain/monodomain formalism or through reduced source models, yielding synthetic body-surface potentials that can be compared with standard ECG leads. Foundational analyses of electrocardiographic forward theory established how source representation, torso inhomogeneity, and atrial position jointly shape surface potentials, thereby motivating anatomically grounded atrial-torso modeling for P-wave studies ref [108], ref [109].

For P-wave synthesis, atrial models are typically embedded in realistic torso geometries and coupled to lead-specific transfer matrices so that localized changes in conduction, anisotropy, or activation origin can be translated into amplitude, duration, and axis changes on the ECG. Experimental-computational studies of atrial activation and body-surface mapping showed that right- and left-atrial contributions are temporally overlapping and nonlinearly filtered by torso volume conduction, limiting direct inference from lead morphology alone ref [110], ref [111]. More recent image-based simulations have exploited this framework to reproduce normal and abnormal P waves, including the effects of interatrial block, Bachmann bundle conduction, and altered pulmonary-vein/left-atrial activation sequences ref [112], ref [113].

A key value of forward modeling in the present context is mechanistic disambiguation: distinct atrial activation patterns can generate similar surface P waves, whereas subtle substrate alterations may become detectable only after lead synthesis. Studies combining patient-specific anatomy with inverse/forward ECG pipelines have therefore emphasized uncertainty quantification in geometry, fiber orientation, and electrode placement when interpreting simulated P-wave variability ref [114], ref [115]. This makes forward ECG synthesis a central component of simulation frameworks aimed at explaining beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation under sinus rhythm and atrial remodeling.

subsections.section_title: Atrial Simulation Frameworks for Studying P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation of sinus rhythm under atrial fibrillation remodeling
subsections.content:
Simulation studies of sinus rhythm under atrial fibrillation (AF) remodeling use chronic AF-induced changes in ionic currents, conduction, and atrial structure to test how a sinus impulse is transformed before any overt arrhythmia is present. Human atrial cell models parameterized for AF remodeling typically incorporate reduced ICaL and Ito, altered IK1 and other repolarizing currents, and shortened action potential duration, following experimentally grounded formulations such as the Courtemanche model and its AF-remodeled variants ref [116], ref [117]. These remodeled membrane dynamics provide the substrate for examining whether beat-to-beat or region-to-region differences in recovery and source–sink balance can already perturb atrial activation sequences and therefore P-wave morphology during nominal sinus rhythm.

At tissue and organ scale, AF remodeling is commonly represented not only by electrophysiological shortening but also by slowed, heterogeneous conduction and fibrosis-related discontinuities. Population and patient-derived simulations have shown that fibrosis can redirect sinus activation, promote local conduction delay, and amplify inter-atrial asynchrony, thereby broadening or fractionating simulated P waves even in the absence of sustained AF ref [101], ref [118]. Modeling studies further indicate that pulmonary-vein and posterior-wall fibrosis are especially influential because they disturb Bachmann bundle-mediated propagation and left atrial breakthrough patterns, mechanisms that are difficult to isolate clinically ref [119], ref [120].

These frameworks are particularly valuable for separating electrical from structural contributors to abnormal sinus P waves. Multi-scale simulations suggest that electrical remodeling alone often shortens local refractoriness without reproducing the full extent of clinical P-wave prolongation, whereas combined ionic, conductive, and fibrotic remodeling better matches the abnormal morphology and duration seen in AF patients ref [121], ref [122]. Such results support the view that P-wave variability in AF-prone atria is a systems-level expression of diffuse remodeling rather than a simple marker of one isolated substrate component ref [123].

subsections.section_title: Atrial Simulation Frameworks for Studying P-Wave Morphology Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Sensitivity and perturbation analyses
subsections.content:
Sensitivity and perturbation analyses are particularly valuable in atrial simulation because P-wave morphology is a weak, spatially integrated signal whose features can change substantially under small variations in activation origin, conduction anisotropy, tissue coupling, and torso transfer. In practice, these studies quantify how uncertainty in electrophysiological and anatomical parameters propagates to P-wave duration, axis, terminal force, and interlead morphology. Variability analyses in computational electrophysiology have increasingly moved from one-factor-at-a-time perturbations toward global uncertainty quantification and emulator-based approaches, enabling the ranking of influential parameters and the identification of nonlinear interactions that would be difficult to infer clinically ref [124], ref [125].

Within atrial models, perturbing conduction velocity, fiber orientation, anisotropy ratio, and regional action-potential properties has shown that activation-sequence descriptors are often more influential for body-surface P-wave morphology than moderate changes in local repolarization kinetics. This is consistent with broader cardiac sensitivity studies demonstrating marked ECG dependence on tissue conductivities, geometry, and source–sink organization ref [126], ref [127]. In anatomically detailed atrial simulations, uncertainty in Bachmann bundle properties, interatrial connections, and sinoatrial exit sites is especially relevant because these factors govern left–right atrial synchrony and therefore the polarity and notching of the simulated P wave ref [128], ref [129].

Methodologically, variance-based indices, polynomial-chaos expansions, and Gaussian-process emulators provide efficient surrogates for expensive forward simulations and support population-level exploration of remodeling scenarios ref [124], ref [125], ref [130]. Such frameworks are useful for studying sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation remodeling, where fibrosis burden, gap-junctional uncoupling, and slowed conduction can be perturbed jointly to separate robust from model-specific determinants of beat-to-beat morphology variability ref [129], ref [101]. A key lesson across studies is that sensitivity is output-dependent: parameters controlling activation timing dominate P-wave onset, duration, and terminal components, whereas torso and electrode uncertainties more strongly affect amplitudes and lead-specific morphology ref [126], ref [130], ref [131].

subsections.section_title: Signal Characterization and Quantification of P-Wave Beat-to-Beat Variability
subsections.subsection_title: ECG preprocessing and P-wave delineation
subsections.content:
Accurate characterization of P-wave beat-to-beat variability depends first on robust preprocessing, because atrial activity is low in amplitude and easily distorted by baseline wander, muscle noise, power-line interference, and residual ventricular activity. Standard ECG cleaning therefore combines band-pass filtering and baseline correction, but the chosen cutoff frequencies can materially reshape P-wave onset, offset, and terminal force, especially in prolonged or biphasic morphologies. Reviews of computerized ECG analysis and practical delineation studies have emphasized that preprocessing choices are not merely technical details; they directly influence fiducial localization and downstream morphology metrics ref [132], ref [133].

P-wave delineation has been approached with derivative-based detectors, wavelet methods, and multi-lead rule-based algorithms. Wavelet-based ECG delineators are widely used because they provide multiscale localization of low-amplitude onsets and offsets and have been validated for fiducial detection in standard databases ref [134], ref [135]. For atrial-specific analysis, multi-lead strategies are especially important, since the earliest onset and latest offset may occur in different leads; this principle underlies recommendations to derive global P-wave duration from all simultaneously recorded leads rather than from a single channel ref [136], ref [137]. Signal averaging can further improve delineation precision in sinus rhythm, although it may suppress genuine short-term variability if applied indiscriminately ref [138].

Additional preprocessing is often required when ectopy, PR-segment drift, or overlapping T and U waves contaminate atrial segments, and the challenge becomes greater in ambulatory recordings or in patients with atrial remodeling. High-resolution or body-surface mapping studies show that improved spatial sampling and careful temporal alignment enhance visualization of subtle atrial activation patterns, but they also underscore the lack of standardized pipelines across datasets ref [139], ref [140]. Consequently, comparisons of beat-to-beat P-wave variability across studies should always be interpreted in light of the specific preprocessing, lead selection, and delineation protocol used.

subsections.section_title: Signal Characterization and Quantification of P-Wave Beat-to-Beat Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Morphological descriptors of the P-wave
subsections.content:
Morphological descriptors of the P-wave seek to convert a low-amplitude, often noisy atrial signal into features that reflect activation timing, conduction anisotropy, and interatrial propagation. The most established descriptors remain duration, peak and mean amplitude, area, and polarity across leads, because they are directly linked to atrial depolarization time and the spatial orientation of the atrial dipole ref [141], ref [142]. Clinical electrocardiography also uses contour-based categories such as notching, biphasic shape, and terminal force in V1 to capture left atrial abnormality and altered interatrial conduction, with the classical Morris index remaining a widely used example ref [143], ref [144].

Beyond these scalar measures, modern analyses emphasize shape-sensitive representations. Principal component analysis has been used to summarize interlead P-wave morphology and derive indices of atrial complexity from the dominant and residual components ref [139]. Time-warping and beat-template approaches compare each beat to a reference waveform and quantify local deformations in onset, peak, and offset timing, thereby separating amplitude variation from true morphological change. Related vectorcardiographic descriptors, including P-loop magnitude, area, and spatial orientation, provide a compact spatial characterization that is less dependent on any single lead and has shown utility in atrial substrate assessment ref [145], ref [146].

For beat-to-beat variability studies, descriptor choice strongly conditions interpretation. Simple interval and amplitude features are robust and reproducible but may miss subtle redistribution of energy within the waveform. Conversely, higher-dimensional descriptors such as wavelet coefficients, eigenwave features, or interlead correlation patterns are more sensitive to localized conduction changes, although they are also more vulnerable to delineation error and preprocessing choices ref [147], ref [148]. Accordingly, most studies benefit from combining physiologically interpretable descriptors with data-driven shape summaries to capture both global atrial conduction delay and fine-grained morphological instability.

subsections.section_title: Signal Characterization and Quantification of P-Wave Beat-to-Beat Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Beat-to-beat variability metrics
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat P-wave variability is quantified by metrics that compare successive atrial depolarization waveforms in either the time or transformed domain. Simple descriptors include cycle-to-cycle changes in P-wave duration, area, amplitude, and axis, but these are often insufficient because small temporal misalignments can masquerade as morphology change. Accordingly, several studies have emphasized template-based or pairwise waveform dissimilarity measures after alignment, including correlation coefficients, normalized root-mean-square error, and time-warping approaches originally developed for ECG morphology comparison ref [149], ref [150]. In noisy ambulatory recordings, robust averaging and fiducial-consistent registration are therefore integral parts of the variability metric rather than merely preprocessing.

A complementary class of metrics represents variability as dispersion within a beat ensemble. Methods based on principal component analysis summarize how much of the P-wave beat ensemble is captured by dominant modes, with residual variance interpreted as morphological instability; related subspace ideas were formalized for ECG wave analysis by Laguna and colleagues and later generalized for ECG variability studies ref [151], ref [152]. In multilead settings, spatial descriptors such as beat-to-beat changes in the P-wave vector or loop morphology can capture atrial conduction heterogeneity that is not visible in single-lead amplitude measures ref [153], ref [154]. Entropy-based and symbolic-dynamics measures have also been explored to separate structured variability from random fluctuation, especially when atrial ectopy or autonomic modulation introduces nonstationary behavior ref [155].

For simulation-to-clinic comparisons, metric choice strongly affects interpretation. Pointwise measures are sensitive to sampling rate, delineation uncertainty, and baseline residuals, whereas shape-preserving distances and low-dimensional manifold summaries are better suited to comparing synthetic and clinical ensembles with different absolute amplitudes ref [150], ref [152], ref [156]. Regardless of formulation, useful beat-to-beat metrics should report both within-subject dispersion and estimator reliability, since repeatability limits have long been recognized as central when quantifying subtle ECG morphology variability ref [157].

subsections.section_title: Signal Characterization and Quantification of P-Wave Beat-to-Beat Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Temporal and spatial representation of variability
subsections.content:
Temporal representation of P-wave beat-to-beat variability concerns how morphology changes are organized across successive atrial activations rather than summarized by a single average template. Time-aligned ensemble approaches, principal-component descriptions, and beat-indexed trajectories in low-dimensional feature space are commonly used to distinguish random fluctuation from structured modulation related to autonomic tone, respiration, or intermittent conduction changes. The logic parallels established analyses of repolarization and depolarization variability in vectorcardiographic space, where beat sequence and trajectory geometry provide information beyond scalar interval measures ref [158], ref [159]. In atrial analysis, such temporal encodings are especially important because subtle shifts in onset, terminal force, and inter-lead correlation may precede overt atrial arrhythmia ref [160], ref [30].

Spatial representation addresses how variability is distributed across leads or over reconstructed atrial activation fields. Standard 12-lead ECG studies often map beat-to-beat changes in amplitude, duration, axis, or terminal negativity to infer anisotropic conduction and regional activation delay ref [161], ref [162]. More explicit spatial models use body-surface potential mapping or electrocardiographic imaging to represent atrial depolarization as evolving wavefront patterns, allowing variability to be localized to specific atrial regions and conduction pathways ref [139], ref [163]. Simulation studies are particularly valuable here because they provide access to transmembrane and epicardial activation sequences, enabling direct comparison between source-level perturbations and their projection into lead-dependent P-wave variability ref [164].

A key methodological issue is that temporal and spatial representations are not interchangeable: temporal averaging can suppress spatially localized instability, whereas spatial aggregation across leads can obscure coherent beat-to-beat dynamics. Consequently, robust characterization increasingly combines beat-resolved temporal statistics with multilead or vector representations, so that variability is interpreted jointly as a sequence and as a distributed atrial conduction pattern.

subsections.section_title: Signal Characterization and Quantification of P-Wave Beat-to-Beat Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative analysis between simulated and clinical signals
subsections.content:
Comparisons between simulated and clinical P-wave variability are valuable because they separate controllable mechanistic perturbations from the confounding effects of noise, lead placement, and inter-subject anatomy. In silico atrial models have shown that conduction velocity heterogeneity, fibrosis distribution, and altered activation pathways can reproduce clinically plausible changes in P-wave duration and morphology, providing a mechanistic basis for ECG observations of atrial remodeling and arrhythmia susceptibility [1,2]. At the same time, body-surface manifestations depend strongly on torso conduction and atrial geometry, so agreement should be judged not only on waveform appearance but also on lead-dependent spatial patterns [3,4].

A recurrent finding is that simulations offer high internal consistency and precise ground truth for activation timing, whereas clinical recordings capture broader variability arising from respiration, autonomic tone, electrode repositioning, and imperfect delineation. This mismatch complicates direct comparison of beat-to-beat metrics: variability that is meaningful in patient ECGs may reflect extracardiac or acquisition-related factors absent from idealized simulations. Consequently, several studies have advocated population-based or personalized pipelines that combine atrial electrophysiology with realistic anatomical models and forward calculations to improve correspondence with measured P waves [4,5]. Such frameworks are especially useful for testing whether specific substrate alterations generate the same variability signatures seen in atrial fibrillation risk phenotypes [6,7].

Methodologically, the most informative comparisons use common feature spaces across domains, such as duration, terminal force, correlation-based morphology dispersion, and vectorcardiographic descriptors, rather than relying solely on visual similarity. Recent digital-twin and statistical-shape approaches further suggest that uncertainty quantification is essential: multiple parameter combinations can yield similar surface P waves, limiting inverse interpretation from ECG alone [5,8]. Thus, comparative analysis is strongest when simulations are treated as hypothesis-generating tools constrained by clinical data, rather than as direct surrogates for patient-specific ground truth [3,8].

subsections.section_title: Signal Characterization and Quantification of P-Wave Beat-to-Beat Variability
subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in reproducibility and standardization
subsections.content:
Reproducibility in P-wave beat-to-beat variability analysis is limited by heterogeneity at every stage of the pipeline: lead selection, filtering, fiducial definition, ensemble alignment, and handling of low-amplitude or merged atrial activity. The P wave is especially vulnerable to preprocessing choices because its amplitude is small relative to noise and baseline wander, so modest differences in high-pass filtering or delineation rules can alter onset/offset timing and morphology metrics materially. Existing standards for ECG acquisition and automated interpretation provide important foundations, but they were not designed specifically for variability-sensitive atrial morphology studies, leaving substantial methodological latitude across datasets and laboratories ref [136], ref [172], ref [173].

A second challenge is the lack of standardized descriptors and reporting conventions. Studies alternately use duration, amplitude, axis, area, wavelet coefficients, principal components, dynamic time warping distances, or template-correlation measures, often without harmonized definitions or uncertainty estimates. The broader reproducibility crisis in computational physiology has highlighted the need for explicit metadata, versioned workflows, and sharable code and annotations ref [174], ref [175]. For ECG, recommendations on measurement standards and data formats exist, yet interoperability between acquisition systems, annotation tools, and simulation outputs remains incomplete ref [176], ref [177].

Standardization is further complicated when simulated and clinical signals are compared. In silico studies can provide perfectly segmented atrial activity, whereas clinical ECGs embed respiration, motion, electrode variability, and ventricular overlap; without common benchmark tasks, reported variability may reflect pipeline differences more than physiology. Community resources such as PhysioNet and the FAIR data principles offer practical routes toward reproducible benchmarking, but dedicated shared datasets with repeated sinus-rhythm recordings, consensus P-wave annotations, and agreed evaluation metrics are still needed ref [178], ref [179].

Overall, progress will depend on minimum reporting standards tailored to atrial variability studies: acquisition settings, lead configuration, delineation criteria, exclusion rules, variability metric definitions, and statistical treatment of within-subject repetition. Such standardization would improve comparability across studies and make claims about atrial conduction dynamics more interpretable.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Clinical Applications of Atrial Simulation Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Early identification of atrial cardiomyopathy
subsections.content:
Atrial simulations provide a mechanistic framework for detecting atrial cardiomyopathy before sustained arrhythmia becomes clinically apparent. By linking P-wave morphology, duration, and beat-to-beat variability to substrate features such as slowed conduction, anisotropy, atrial dilatation, and regional fibrosis, modeling studies suggest that subtle surface-ECG changes may reflect early structural-electrical remodeling rather than nonspecific conduction noise. This concept aligns with the broader clinical redefinition of atrial cardiomyopathy as a spectrum of architectural, contractile, and electrophysiological alterations that may precede overt atrial fibrillation or stroke risk ref [180].

Translationally, the strongest candidate mechanisms are fibrotic remodeling and conduction heterogeneity. Human and imaging studies have shown that left atrial fibrosis is associated with sinus-rhythm conduction abnormalities and adverse outcomes ref [181], while delayed-enhancement MRI can localize fibrotic substrate linked to arrhythmia vulnerability ref [59]. Surface ECG markers thought to reflect this substrate, particularly advanced interatrial block and prolonged or abnormal P-wave morphology, have been associated with incident atrial fibrillation, ischemic stroke, and mortality ref [38], ref [182]. Simulation studies are valuable here because they can test whether specific combinations of fibrosis burden, myofiber disarray, and preferential conduction block are sufficient to reproduce these P-wave phenotypes.

Accordingly, simulated P-wave variability may evolve into an inexpensive digital biomarker for preclinical atrial disease, especially when integrated with echocardiographic or MRI-derived anatomy. This is clinically attractive because electroanatomic evidence indicates that low-voltage, fibrotic atrial substrate can already be present in patients without documented atrial fibrillation ref [183], and because fibrosis burden predicts recurrence after ablation ref [184]. More generally, atrial cardiomyopathy has emerged as a plausible substrate linking embolic stroke of undetermined source and later atrial fibrillation ref [185], making early ECG-informed identification a potential avenue for preventive phenotyping and surveillance.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Clinical Applications of Atrial Simulation Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Prediction of atrial fibrillation onset and recurrence
subsections.content:
Atrial simulation studies suggest that beat-to-beat and spatial variability in the P wave can act as a preclinical marker of the substrate that later sustains atrial fibrillation (AF). Mechanistically, models show that modest combinations of slowed conduction, anisotropy, fibrosis, and regional action-potential heterogeneity can amplify dispersion of activation without requiring overt arrhythmia, providing a plausible bridge between subtle surface-ECG changes and future AF susceptibility. This interpretation is consistent with clinical observations linking abnormal P-wave morphology, prolonged P-wave duration, and advanced interatrial block to incident AF in population and patient cohorts ref [186], ref [187], ref [21].

The same rationale extends to recurrence prediction after cardioversion or catheter ablation. Simulation-derived metrics of conduction reserve and activation fragility imply that patients with larger latent substrate heterogeneity should exhibit greater P-wave variability even in sinus rhythm, and therefore a higher probability of post-procedural AF re-initiation. Clinically, ECG studies have associated P-wave indices and signal-averaged atrial activation abnormalities with AF recurrence after ablation or cardioversion ref [188], ref [189], ref [190]. More recent work using noninvasive computational modeling has further shown that patient-specific fibrotic atrial substrates reconstructed from imaging can predict arrhythmia inducibility and recurrence risk, reinforcing the translational value of substrate-informed biomarkers ref [101], ref [191].

For translational use, the main opportunity is to combine simulated sensitivity analyses with routinely available ECG features to distinguish transient triggers from a persistent arrhythmogenic substrate. Such an approach could improve timing of intensified rhythm monitoring, identify patients needing earlier intervention, and contextualize recurrence risk beyond conventional clinical scores alone. However, evidence remains largely associative, and prospective studies are still needed to test whether simulation-informed P-wave variability markers add independent predictive value over established ECG and imaging predictors ref [21], ref [191], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Clinical Applications of Atrial Simulation Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Patient stratification and phenotype discovery
subsections.content:
Atrial simulations provide a mechanistic basis for stratifying patients beyond conventional ECG or imaging descriptors by linking P-wave variability to underlying conduction phenotypes. In particular, computational and electrocardiographic studies indicate that interatrial block, anisotropic conduction, and regional fibrosis can generate distinct P-wave morphologies and activation patterns, suggesting that apparently similar clinical rhythms may arise from different substrates ref [192], ref [193], ref [194]. This is important for phenotype discovery because it supports grouping patients according to latent electrophysiological mechanisms rather than only by AF history or atrial size.

Model-informed phenotyping is especially valuable in heterogeneous entities such as atrial cardiomyopathy. Simulation frameworks incorporating patient-specific anatomy and fibrosis distributions have shown that localized fibrotic remodeling alters activation routes and body-surface signatures in ways that may help identify substrate-dominant versus conduction-dominant phenotypes ref [195], ref [196]. Complementary work combining atrial imaging, electro-anatomical mapping, and computational modeling has further suggested that fibrosis burden alone is insufficient; its spatial organization and interaction with fiber architecture are critical for differentiating clinically meaningful subgroups ref [13], ref [197].

These ideas align with broader data-driven efforts to redefine AF-related disease states through multidomain phenomapping. Cluster analyses integrating clinical variables, imaging, and electrophysiology have already identified reproducible AF phenotypes with different outcomes ref [198], while machine-learning analyses of atrial structure and function support the existence of latent atrial disease classes ref [199]. A translational opportunity for P-wave simulation studies is therefore to supply interpretable mechanistic features that can anchor such clusters, improving biological plausibility and potentially enabling phenotype-specific surveillance or treatment selection.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Clinical Applications of Atrial Simulation Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Guidance for personalized modeling and therapy planning
subsections.content:
Atrial simulations are increasingly used to translate P-wave variability into patient-specific models that support therapy planning. In this framework, body-surface ECG features are combined with imaging-derived atrial anatomy, fibrosis burden, and conduction properties to infer individualized activation patterns and substrate heterogeneity, thereby linking noninvasive electrical phenotypes to actionable mechanisms ref [200], ref [201]. Such models are particularly attractive when invasive mapping is unavailable or incomplete, because they can test how regional slowing, anisotropy, or fibrotic remodeling shape P-wave morphology and beat-to-beat variability before intervention ref [202], ref [203].

For catheter ablation, personalized atrial models have shown value in identifying arrhythmogenic regions and in comparing candidate lesion sets in silico. Studies using MRI-informed left atrial models demonstrated that fibrosis distribution can localize re-entrant drivers and predict where ablation may terminate atrial fibrillation, while digital-twin style simulations have been proposed to prospectively optimize treatment strategy for individual patients ref [204], ref [205], ref [206]. Although most work has focused on AF maintenance rather than P-wave variability per se, the same mechanistic framework suggests that simulated P-wave signatures could help select patients for pulmonary vein isolation alone versus broader substrate modification.

A similar logic extends to pacing and surgical planning. Computational analyses have shown that interatrial conduction pathways, including Bachmann’s bundle, strongly influence atrial activation and surface P-wave expression, implying that model-based assessment of conduction reserve may inform atrial lead placement or prediction of post-procedural conduction disturbances ref [207], ref [3]. The main translational challenge is robust personalization: uncertainty in fiber architecture, fibrosis representation, and ECG forward modeling still limits confidence in patient-level therapeutic recommendations.

subsections.section_title: Translational and Clinical Applications of Atrial Simulation Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Integration with machine learning and digital health tools
subsections.content:
Atrial simulation studies can provide mechanistically grounded features for machine-learning pipelines, helping bridge the gap between subtle P-wave variability and clinically actionable risk markers. In this role, biophysical models act as data generators, weak labels, or priors that constrain inference from noisy ECGs, rather than simply replacing statistical classifiers. This hybrid strategy is particularly attractive for digital biomarkers of atrial remodeling because simulated conduction slowing, anisotropy, and fibrosis distributions can be linked to surface P-wave descriptors that are otherwise difficult to interpret from observational data alone ref [208], ref [209].

Recent AI work on ECG-based phenotyping illustrates the translational opportunity. Deep neural networks can infer latent cardiac structure and rhythm risk directly from sinus-rhythm ECGs, including future atrial fibrillation and atrial structural abnormalities ref [210], ref [211], ref [212]. Simulation-derived libraries of P-wave morphologies could improve these models by augmenting underrepresented phenotypes, stress-testing domain shift, and enabling more interpretable feature attribution. Relatedly, computational frameworks for “digital twins” and in silico trials provide a pathway for integrating simulated atrial conduction phenotypes with patient-specific data streams from ECG patches, wearables, and electronic health records ref [213], ref [214].

However, translation into digital health tools requires careful validation. Signal quality, lead placement variability, demographic imbalance, and mismatch between simplified atrial models and real-world pathology can all degrade generalization. Reporting standards for AI and a staged evaluation pipeline—from retrospective ECG repositories to prospective ambulatory monitoring—are therefore essential if simulation-informed P-wave biomarkers are to become trustworthy components of screening, remote monitoring, or decision support systems ref [215], ref [216].

subsections.section_title: Translational and Clinical Applications of Atrial Simulation Studies
subsections.subsection_title: Limitations of current translational evidence
subsections.content:
Current translational evidence linking atrial simulation-derived P-wave variability to clinical decision-making remains limited by model fidelity and validation depth. Many studies still rely on idealized atrial geometries, simplified fiber architecture, and uncertain representations of inter-individual conduction heterogeneity, despite longstanding evidence that activation patterns are highly sensitive to anatomy and anisotropy ref [217], ref [218]. Even when detailed image-based atrial models are used, parameter identifiability is weak: multiple combinations of fibrosis burden, conduction velocity, and cellular remodeling can reproduce similar surface ECG signatures, complicating mechanistic interpretation and biomarker specificity ref [219], ref [220].

A second limitation is the gap between mechanistic plausibility and prospective clinical utility. Atrial fibrosis and structural remodeling are clinically relevant, but their relationship to ECG phenotypes is indirect and influenced by noise, lead placement, autonomic state, and comorbidity ref [30], ref [59]. This contributes to limited external validation and uncertain generalizability across cohorts, acquisition systems, and rhythm states. More broadly, contemporary reviews of digital and computational cardiology emphasize that reproducibility, uncertainty quantification, and regulatory-grade evidence remain underdeveloped for in silico biomarkers intended for patient stratification or therapy planning ref [221], ref [222].

Accordingly, stronger translational evidence will require multi-center datasets with standardized ECG and imaging pipelines, patient-specific model calibration, and prospective studies testing whether simulation-informed P-wave markers add incremental value over established clinical predictors. Community efforts toward verification, validation, and credibility assessment provide an important framework, but they have not yet been fully implemented in most atrial electrophysiology studies ref [222], ref [223].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Gaps, Scoping Review Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Landscape of existing atrial simulation studies
subsections.content:
The atrial simulation literature has evolved from idealized, monodomain studies of wave propagation toward multiscale, anatomically detailed frameworks that explicitly represent chamber geometry, fiber architecture, and regional electrophysiological heterogeneity. Foundational work established the feasibility of whole-atria activation modeling and demonstrated how anisotropy and structural detail shape activation sequence and reentry dynamics, thereby creating a basis for interpreting body-surface signatures such as the P wave and its beat-to-beat variability ref [224], ref [225]. Subsequent biophysically detailed cell and tissue models further expanded the field by embedding human atrial ionic formulations within 3-dimensional atrial anatomies, enabling systematic testing of conduction slowing, refractoriness, and remodeling scenarios relevant to sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation substrates ref [226], ref [227].

A second major strand has focused on personalization and inverse modeling. Statistical shape and fiber models, image-based reconstruction, and patient-specific electrophysiology calibration have been used to generate individualized atrial digital twins and to explore how anatomical variability alters activation pathways and electrocardiographic output ref [228], ref [107]. Parallel efforts in electrocardiographic imaging and forward modeling have strengthened links between simulated atrial activation and measurable surface potentials, although these studies often prioritize activation timing or arrhythmia localization over subtle beat-to-beat morphology fluctuation ref [139].

Overall, the current landscape is rich in mechanistic sophistication but uneven in its direct relevance to beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation. Many studies emphasize atrial fibrillation initiation, rotor dynamics, or ablation planning rather than repeated sinus beats under varying autonomic, loading, or ectopic conditions ref [227], ref [229]. More recent personalized atrial modeling studies indicate that clinically interpretable atrial biomarkers can emerge from these frameworks, but dedicated simulation paradigms for short-term P-wave variability remain comparatively sparse ref [107], ref [230].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Gaps, Scoping Review Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Common assumptions and sources of bias
subsections.content:
A recurring assumption in atrial simulations is that P-wave morphology can be inferred from a small set of idealized atrial geometries, homogeneous tissue properties, and fixed torso conductivities. This simplification improves tractability but can systematically underestimate inter-subject variability in activation pathways and body-surface projection. Population analyses have shown substantial anatomical heterogeneity in human atria, including fiber architecture and wall thickness, while biophysical studies demonstrate that fibrosis and conduction anisotropy strongly reshape activation timing and electrogram morphology, making generic models vulnerable to structural bias ref [231], ref [232], ref [233].

A second source of bias arises from how excitation is initiated and represented. Many studies prescribe a single sinus node breakthrough or deterministic interatrial conduction route, despite evidence that SAN exit sites and preferential pathways are variable and can shift with autonomic tone, disease, or pacing conditions ref [234], ref [235]. In parallel, reduced-order atrial action-potential formulations may reproduce activation sequences while neglecting repolarization and restitution effects that can influence beat-to-beat waveform subtlety; the broader cardiac modeling literature has long warned that parameter identifiability and model discrepancy can be substantial when observations are sparse ref [236], ref [237].

Methodological bias is also introduced during validation. Simulations are often compared only with standard 12-lead ECGs or averaged beats, whereas inverse and forward studies indicate that electrode placement, torso inhomogeneity, filtering, and annotation choices can materially alter observed P-wave morphology ref [238], ref [239]. Consequently, apparent agreement may reflect compensating errors rather than correct atrial mechanisms, underscoring the need to report uncertainty, sensitivity analyses, and preprocessing decisions explicitly.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Gaps, Scoping Review Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Need for multimodal and longitudinal validation
subsections.content:
A major limitation of current work on beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation is that validation is often confined to a single signal domain, most commonly the surface ECG. Yet atrial activation patterns are only indirectly observed in the P wave, and inverse inferences remain non-unique. Multimodal validation should therefore link simulated and measured phenomena across body-surface recordings, intracardiac electrograms, electroanatomic maps, and structural imaging, so that morphology variation is assessed against both electrical timing and anatomical substrate constraints. The feasibility and value of such integrative pipelines have been demonstrated in personalized atrial modeling frameworks combining imaging with electrophysiology and ECG-based validation ref [240], ref [241], ref [206].

For this topic, multimodal datasets are especially important because beat-to-beat changes may reflect several interacting mechanisms: shifts in sinoatrial exit, anisotropic conduction, functional block, respiration-related motion, and evolving atrial fibrosis. Late gadolinium enhancement MRI and patient-specific geometric reconstructions have already shown potential for relating atrial substrate heterogeneity to conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia propensity ref [13], ref [242]. Likewise, ECG imaging and body-surface mapping provide intermediate spatial scales that can help determine whether a simulated P-wave change corresponds to a true alteration in activation sequence rather than to lead placement, filtering, or torso-model assumptions ref [243], ref [244].

Longitudinal validation is equally necessary. Most studies compare models with data from a single session, despite the fact that atrial conduction properties and P-wave indices evolve with aging, ablation, autonomic state, and disease progression. Longitudinal cohorts have shown that P-wave characteristics predict incident atrial fibrillation and other adverse outcomes over time ref [21], ref [245]. Future simulation studies should therefore be evaluated not only cross-sectionally, but also for their ability to reproduce within-subject temporal trajectories, treatment-induced remodeling, and day-to-day variability under standardized repeated-acquisition protocols.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Gaps, Scoping Review Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Standardized reporting and benchmarking frameworks
subsections.content:
A major barrier to cumulative progress in simulations of beat-to-beat P-wave morphology is the absence of a shared reporting standard. At minimum, studies should document atrial anatomy source, fiber assignment strategy, conductivity formulation, ionic model version, stimulation protocol, torso coupling assumptions, and the precise definition of the P-wave metrics being analyzed. Existing cardiac electrophysiology guidance already points toward such transparency: the Cardiac Physiome model-description standards and the MICEE reporting recommendations were designed to improve reproducibility and parameter traceability in computational electrophysiology ref [246], ref [175], while broader reproducibility statements in biomedical modeling emphasize complete disclosure of equations, parameterization, and code provenance ref [247].

Benchmarking should extend beyond model description to task-specific evaluation. For atrial simulations, this implies community datasets and reference protocols that compare activation time, conduction pathways, body-surface P-wave morphology, and sensitivity to mesh resolution or fibrosis representation across platforms. Lessons can be drawn from the open CARP framework and its emphasis on reproducible in silico experiments, as well as from the credibility-assessment framework ASME V&V 40, which formalizes context-of-use, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification for computational models in medicine ref [248], ref [249]. In parallel, reporting should distinguish calibration, internal validation, and external validation, following practical recommendations for transparent validation of patient-specific electrophysiology models ref [250].

A useful next step would be a benchmarking schema tailored to P-wave variation, combining open anatomical models, standardized sinus-node and ectopic pacing scenarios, agreed preprocessing pipelines for simulated and recorded ECGs, and uncertainty reporting for both electrophysiological and geometric parameters. Recent consensus efforts around verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification in multiscale cardiac models provide an appropriate foundation for such a framework ref [251], and FAIR-oriented principles for reusable digital assets should guide model, data, and workflow dissemination ref [179].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Gaps, Scoping Review Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Bridging mechanistic modeling and clinical implementation
subsections.content:
Bridging mechanistic atrial modeling to clinical use requires moving beyond proof-of-concept simulations toward workflows that are patient-specific, computationally tractable, and interpretable at the bedside. The broader translational pathway is already visible in ventricular modeling, where personalized digital hearts have been used for arrhythmia risk stratification and therapy planning, illustrating how imaging, electrophysiology, and simulation can be integrated into clinically actionable pipelines ref [252], ref [253]. For beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation, an analogous framework would link anatomy, fiber architecture, conduction anisotropy, and regional electrophysiological heterogeneity to observable surface-ECG features, while explicitly quantifying uncertainty in inverse and forward solutions ref [254], ref [255].

A key implementation challenge is that clinical ECG phenotypes are low dimensional, noisy, and often nonspecific relative to the large parameter space of atrial models. This makes identifiability, calibration, and validation central concerns rather than secondary technical details. Recent work on uncertainty quantification and credibility assessment in cardiac modeling emphasizes the need for rigorous model qualification, sensitivity analysis, and context-of-use definitions before clinical deployment ref [256], ref [257]. In parallel, machine-learning approaches can help emulate expensive simulations or assist parameter inference, but they should be constrained by physiology to avoid accurate-yet-nonmechanistic predictions ref [258].

A practical research agenda is therefore to develop hybrid mechanistic-data-driven pipelines that are prospectively tested in clinically relevant tasks, such as identifying atrial remodeling substrates, predicting progression toward atrial fibrillation, or tailoring ablation planning. Efforts toward standardized verification and validation in computational physiology provide an important foundation for this transition ref [259], while recent reviews on digital twins in cardiology highlight the regulatory, interoperability, and workflow issues that must be resolved if atrial simulations are to inform routine interpretation of P-wave variability ref [260].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Gaps, Scoping Review Considerations, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging research opportunities
subsections.content:
A key opportunity is to move from static, single-beat atrial models toward patient-specific digital twins that explicitly represent beat-to-beat variability in conduction, repolarization, autonomic tone, and atrial mechanics. Recent personalized atrial modeling frameworks for arrhythmia simulation suggest that individualized anatomy and fibrosis distributions can be reconstructed from clinical data and used to probe latent mechanisms ref [114], ref [101]. Extending these pipelines to P-wave morphology variation would enable in silico testing of how subtle shifts in sinoatrial exit, preferential conduction, or transient anisotropy translate into surface ECG signatures.

A second direction is multimodal data fusion. Combining body-surface mapping, intracardiac electrograms, electroanatomic mapping, and imaging-based structural priors could substantially improve identifiability of competing mechanisms, building on prior inverse and integrative electrophysiology studies ref [261], ref [262]. Machine-learning tools may be particularly useful when embedded within physics-based workflows rather than used as purely black-box classifiers; hybrid strategies have already shown promise for linking ECG phenotypes with latent substrate properties and future arrhythmic risk ref [263], ref [264].

Finally, future work should address temporal scale and intervention sensitivity. Longitudinal simulations calibrated to repeated ECGs, wearable monitoring, and evolving substrate characterization may clarify whether beat-to-beat P-wave variation is an early marker of atrial remodeling or merely an epiphenomenon. Such studies would align with broader calls for digital twin approaches in cardiology and for mechanistic-computational biomarkers that are prospectively testable in clinical workflows ref [265], ref [221].
